title: First Dixieland on Bourbon Street, Leon Prima's 500 Club
summary: Dixieland for dancing at the 500 Club c. 1947-48; before the war the street played pop and modern styles.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: The Paddock Club has retained their policy throughout the years. Matter of fact, I believe the Paddock was instrumental in setting the jazz reaction off on the, uh, off on the jazz trend, or what there was, off on Bourbon Street. But even before that, 1947 or 1948, uh, Leroy Primer had a club, St. Louis and Bourbon, the 500 Club. And while he presented shows, while he presented shows, he did a, the house policy was for, to have a show. And then the stage would push, push back under the bandstand, and we played for dancing. And Leon, uh, very well known Dixieland Trump, you know, I guess you know his brother, Louis Primer. And we were the first ones on the street, we were the first ones on the street, to present Dixieland tunes. And we would play our Dixieland tunes for dancing. And it was Roy Zimmerman, Monk Hazel, I think he's left us. Uh, Leon Primer and myself, and, uh, we liked the trombone, but we did the Dixieland tunes. Well, shortly after that, I think, you know, or about the time that the Paddock instituted a policy, and tried Dixieland music, and I think Pop Celestan was in there. Is that correct? About 48, 47? You had, actually had Don music for dancing, did you? We did the Dixieland music for dancing. In here?
No, no, it was at the 500 Club. Oh, this was at the 500 Club. This was before you opened your place.

About 47, 1948. So actually, that was the first, now that I know of, that was the first little Dixieland music in this area, in the French Quarter. Because prior to that, before I went to the Army in 42, there were several clubs on the street, and one in particular was the, uh, ballet club. And I had a band in there for a couple of years. But we played for dancing, and we played for shows, but we didn't make any attempt at playing Dixieland music. We played the pop music of the day, you know, for dancing, and of course we played the show numbers. But it was in the Dixieland band, and it, instrumental-wise or anything, you know, three saxophones and one guitar and one trumpet. But, uh, as I said, when I first, Leon Prem, I think opened his club shortly after the war, and he was the first one to put a taste of Dixieland on the street. So just a taste. We'd play five or six tunes, Muscat Ramble, and we'd play Saints, or we'd play, uh, Sensation, something like that. And, uh, for dancing. And then, uh, after a dance set, the show would go on. But that was the first, uh, first time I've run across Dixieland music. I actually played in the French Quarter.

Amazing. Can you remember that before, like in, uh, before the war, can you remember it at all? I mean, there was... Before the war. Or, say, around early, very early 40s, there really wasn't any, any jazz.

No, there was, there was jazz in a sense, but it was, uh, uh, currently the modern jazz. There wasn't any, uh, Dixieland. We played, uh, whatever was, uh, in the vein, all clarinet players emulated, uh, or tried to, Benny Goodman. All the saxophone players were trying to play like Vito Musso. And all the trumpet players were another Harry James. And, uh, the boys that did manage to keep this Dixieland music alive throughout all of these years, they weren't working too often, too regularly. They'd play a funeral, they'd play some socialites for dance somewhere, and, uh, and actually it was pretty thin, uh, I think George Lewis was working on the ribbon. You know?
